claims.text: The starting Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, metastable single-phase solid solution.
Prolonged high-temperature exposure causes diffusion-controlled phase separation in the metastable alloy.
High-temperature exposure nucleates and grows intermetallic precipitates from the metastable matrix.
The precipitated compounds may be Mg-Ti-Zn or similar phases.
Fine intermetallic precipitates act as nucleation sites for continuous protective oxide films.
The protective films may contain stable TiO2 or MgO species formed at precipitate interfaces.
Controlled intermetallic phases and oxide formation can contribute to balancing corrosion behavior in Mg-based materials.
A fine, uniformly dispersed precipitate population retains or improves corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
Prolonged thermal exposure can cause intermetallic phases to coarsen and can generate additional precipitates.
Intermetallic precipitates eventually interconnect after coarsening beyond a critical size or morphology.
Coarsened or interconnected intermetallic phases disrupt uniform passivation and create local electrochemical heterogeneity.
The resulting electrochemical heterogeneity promotes localized galvanic activity and accelerates corrosion and oxidation.
Samples with substantially coarsened and interconnected intermetallic phases will have higher corrosion current density, lower corrosion potential, and less protective oxide scales.
Performance changes from beneficial to detrimental when heat-treatment conditions cross a precipitate-coarsening threshold.
Comparing isothermal treatments at 800 °C and 1200 °C for 1000 hours is proposed to produce distinguishable precipitate states.
TEM, SEM, and XRD can be used to determine precipitate nature, size, distribution, and phase identity after treatment.
Corrosion polarization measurements and oxidation mass-gain and scale analyses are proposed as environmental-performance measurements.

The hypothesis is falsified if precipitate refinement or coarsening does not correlate with the predicted improvement or degradation in corrosion and oxidation performance relative to the initial state.
The precipitate-nucleation kinetics, critical precipitate dimensions, and quantitative relationship between precipitate evolution and oxide-scale characteristics are unresolved.

contradictions.description: The conditions field can be read as placing both air oxidation and aqueous NaCl corrosion within the stated 800–1200 °C service range, whereas the experiment describes heat treatment followed by a separate NaCl polarization test. The temperature and sequencing of the aqueous corrosion exposure are therefore internally unclear.
